title: Ponce's night in jail, Bob Young, spaghetti suppers and Perretti at the Liberty
summary: One long answer covers Ponce's arrest, fishing with Bob Young, the band's spaghetti suppers, Perretti's betting, and taking over the Liberty pit from Max Fink.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: He said, you were thinking of me. I said, how do you know? He said, ESP. I said, ESP, you're drunk. Just like that. Me! Screaming. Then he goes on. And I've got to listen to his war record again. Concussion in the brain. He missed nine jobs and I took it. You're drunk, just like that. Me, screaming. Then he goes on, and I've gotta listen to his war record again. Concussion in the brain. He missed nine jobs, and I took it. But one night, he went off on intermission, didn't come back. I found out he was in jail, got in an automobile accident. We rushed down to Poland Street, we get him out of jail, and we get him out. He says to the death sergeant, he says to him, give me my so-and-so money back, and all you so-and-so, you know? Sergeant says, put him back in the clink. I started to say something, he says, you say anything, I'll put you back in the clink. Oh, I'll let him get out of there quickly, they'll put me in jail. So I let him go. I had to let him go. But I'll tell you that I used him on impossible combinations, because I loved his guitar playing. And when I had a bank with a big, something where it didn't require too much loud music, people could hear it, I would ask Arthur to play a couple of his arrangements, like the world is waiting for the sunrise, and I never heard such chords in my heart. I personally was thrilled to that man's playing. So I know, if they didn't know he was good, they'd just hear you. And he's good today, but his father dropped in his arms a couple of weeks ago, and now they're fixing up the estate and somebody's going to grab a hold of that boy. He's about four feet tall and four feet wide. He's a crack shot with a pistol. And when I used to go fishing, he always carried it up there, I figured they'd shoot me. We used to go fishing together. I powered all my, Bob Yeo, afterwards I put him in the union at 16, he's a builder, but he loves to play music. I believe he played for nothing. I mean, he's, Ernest just told me they're playing a job out of town and Bob's on the job, and I know Bob doesn't need the money. I fish with Bob Young. He's the one that I sent to Dr. Brown because he's nauseated every night. That's wrong, he doesn't get enough sleep. But he always was a nervous rink, and always too thin. But such a splendid gentleman. Such a nice wife, nice family. I love my boys. My band periodically, we'd go down on Neanderth Street, there was a place that we called Maceres, and we'd have a, we'd take some of the performers that we liked, and we'd have a spaghetti supper. And we'd have spaghetti and meatballs and some dago red. And we'd get a room upstairs, you know. Comes at about 40 cents a head. Yeah, I'm like, and Perretti, Perretti could eat a platter full of spaghetti. Perretti was a great guy. He had a lot of rock hands. But he played with me at the Liberty. You see, I took him, any time I could get him, I'd take him. So when I went over to the Liberty to take Max Fink's place, he got some scandal. And I was on, you know, as you say, I was on the staff, I was sure of a job. I directed the orchestra to St. Charles when they had dramatic stop. All I did was play between the acts. So all I had to do was head out to dance books. You could play what you played last night. You know, I'd never have nothing to worry about. And played a curtain up. I knew about enough to play a little thing. Well, the curtain went up, you know. Or if it was rain, or something like the African cannibals, I'd go, da da da da da da, boom, jeep, boom. Great. I was the only one who could think of it, because I had played. I always took Perretti around it. He had bad habits. He'd make a bet of two dollars every intermission, which resulted that at the end of the week he lost more than he made. Couldn't stay away from betting. He said, I'm only betting two bucks. I said, but two bets four times a day is eight dollars a day. You're making forty-four dollars a week. That's all he was getting. That was good money in those days. I bet you. Well, I said, why don't worry about that? It doesn't affect his climate plan. He's actually going to play in my own business. But then I had to put on an overture every week. And Max Fink, when he left there, was playing poet and peasant. Overture. I think he did it to put me on, because I'm the man on the box now. I'm the man with the trumpet. I'm leading the orchestra with the trumpet. And Elmore Ryan, the manager, said, what are you going to play, Johnny? He's playing poet and peasant. I said, I'm going to play poet and peasant.
